description: Herramienta web que hace visible el movimiento de objetos cercanos a la Tierra entre distintas épocas de SPHEREx. Consulta el archivo, descarga recortes de la misma posición y banda en fechas sucesivas, los normaliza y alinea, y los alterna con un slider para revelar el desplazamiento. Caso de estudio: 2026 ED138 (Mani), con movimiento aparente superior a un grado por año.
summary:
SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 near-infrared bands, recording over a billion sources per sweep. Our project asks a simple question: can that archive recover an object that was discovered and then lost?

We built a web tool that queries the SPHEREx archive through IRSA, downloads cutouts of the same field at successive epochs, normalizes and aligns them, and presents them in a viewer with a slider. Fixed stars stay put; anything that moves separates itself. No catalog work, no per-source analysis — the candidate becomes visible to anyone.

Our case study is 2026 ED138, known as Mani, a near-Earth object drifting more than one degree per year across the sky. Using the IRSA Moving Object Search Tool, we found that 365 SPHEREx image frames covered Mani's predicted positions between August 2025 and September 2026. Those frames have never been examined for this object.
details: WHAT IT DOES Our tool queries the SPHEREx archive at IRSA using astroquery (TAP and SIA2), downloads cutouts of the same sky region at successive epochs, normalizes background and signal scale across frames, registers them to a common astrometric frame, and serves them in a viewer where a slider alternates between epochs. A moving object appears to jump between frames while the star field stays fixed. WHY IT MATTERS SPHEREx is a new survey with a very large archive, and almost no work has been done on solar system object recovery with it. A moving-object search is normally a catalog problem requiring per-source extraction across billions of detections. Our approach turns it into a visual problem that anyone can check. THE CASE STUDY: 2026 ED138 (MANI) Mani is a near-Earth object whose apparent motion exceeds one degree per year, measured from our own linear fit to JPL Horizons ephemerides over 2013–2026. We verified with Horizons that its declination stays between −43° and −46°, placing it outside the DES and PS1 footprints in every year we checked. We then ran the IRSA Moving Object Search Tool against the SPHEREx image collection. Result: 365 matched image frames, covering 23 August 2025 to 8 September 2026, with predicted positions between Dec −42.5° and −42.9° and V ≈ 19.8. Several frames place Mani within 0.2° of the field centre, and multiple nights have four exposures of the same field, which is what a difference-imaging search requires. These frames are a list of predicted positions, not confirmed detections: nobody has looked for Mani in them. TOOLS AND DATA Python, astroquery and astropy for archive access, NumPy and Matplotlib for processing, and a static front end for the viewer. NASA DATA SPHEREx data through IRSA: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/applications/spherex/ IRSA Moving Object Search Tool: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/applications/MOST/ JPL Horizons ephemerides: https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/ OTHER DATA Astropy, astroquery, ATLAS Forced Photometry, and the NASA Space Apps challenge statement. CONSIDERATION SPHEREx has 6.2 arcsecond pixels and a per-band 5-sigma point source limit near 18.4 AB mag. Mani is at V ≈ 19.8, so detection is marginal and requires forced photometry at the predicted positions rather than blind search. During the event the IRSA endpoints returned 502 errors, so the live viewer demonstrates its behaviour on synthetic epoch images produced by the same normalization and alignment code; swapping in real cutouts is a one-line change.
projectRefs: NASA Space Apps — Planet X and SPHEREx challenge
